subtype: Approach: ignoring warning signs of burnout [Pitfall]
passage: “Sonali, sit down. I'll tell you something I never told your mother. I'm Chaitanya, your uncle. When I was sixteen I studied for the entrance test from five till midnight. The headaches started in the second month. I turned short-tempered and snapped at my sister for nothing. Every time the coaching bell rang, my stomach turned over with dread. I told myself only weak boys complain, so I pushed on. In exam week I sat down at the desk and my mind went blank. Not tired: empty. I read the same question eleven times. I lost the seat I'd worked a year for. What I regret isn't the seat. It's that for four months I brushed off every sign my own body gave me.”

qa.q: How many times did Chaitanya read the same question in exam week?
What did Chaitanya feel each time the coaching bell rang?
qa.a: Dread: his stomach turned over, and he brushed it off as weakness.

qa.q: At what point in the story could a different choice have changed things?
qa.a: When the headaches began in the second month, telling someone or easing the schedule then might have prevented the collapse, instead of telling himself only weak boys complain.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya's sister have experienced those months?
qa.a: She was snapped at for no reason by a brother who seemed to have lost his patience, and may have felt hurt or worried without knowing why.

grounding: An elder recalls dismissing headaches, irritability and dread as weakness, pushing on and ending in a blank exam week.

subtype: Approach: ignoring warning signs of burnout [Pitfall]
passage:
With her mother away in Patna caring for her grandmother, Indu was running the house and three coaching batches at once. Every morning she woke with a dull headache. She snapped at her little brother over a spilled glass. Walking to the physics batch, her stomach knotted with dread.

"You look terrible," her friend Pallavi said one evening.

"It's nothing. I'm just weak. Toppers don't complain." Indu swallowed two biscuits and kept going.

For four more weeks she pushed through. She stopped telling anyone about the headaches. She told herself dread was laziness.

Then, a week before the half-yearly exams, something just stopped. She sat at her desk with the chemistry book open and couldn't make the words mean anything. She tried for three days. Nothing went in.

She sat the exams in a fog and left half of the physics paper blank.

qa.a: Away in Patna, caring for Indu's grandmother.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling as she walked to the physics batch?
qa.a: She felt dread, her stomach knotting, which she wrongly told herself was laziness.

qa.q: What should Indu have done when the headaches and dread began?
qa.a: Told a parent, teacher or counsellor early and eased the load, and if the headaches kept going or worried anyone, checked with a doctor.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt watching Indu over those weeks?
qa.a: Pallavi was probably worried and a bit helpless, noticing Indu looked terrible but being brushed off.

grounding: Shows a student under extra pressure dismissing headaches, irritability and dread as weakness and pushing on until motivation collapses and exam week passes without focus.

subtype: Approach: ignoring warning signs of burnout [Pitfall]
passage:
In their Noida flat, Divyansh had been going to four coaching classes since March. By August he had headaches most afternoons. He shouted at his sister Sangeeta for using his charger. He felt sick every evening before the maths batch.

"You should tell Mummy," Sangeeta said.

"And say what? That I'm weak?" He took his bag and went.

He kept going. The headaches became normal. He started lying awake. He told himself real students didn't complain.

Then, in the week of his mid-terms, he sat at his desk and felt nothing. Not tired, not stressed. Just empty. He opened his notes and stared at them for an hour. The next day, the same.

He wrote the chemistry paper without remembering half of it. When the results came, he didn't even feel surprised.

Sangeeta found him on the balcony that evening and sat beside him. "Come," she said softly. "Let's tell Mummy together, now." This time he went.

qa.q: Since when had Divyansh been going to four coaching classes?
How did Divyansh feel in the week of his mid-terms?
qa.a: He felt empty and numb, unable to focus on his notes at all.

qa.q: What could Divyansh do now to recover?
qa.a: He could tell his parents and the school counsellor how he has been feeling, reduce the coaching load with them, and see a doctor about the headaches if they keep going.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta have felt sitting beside him on the balcony?
qa.a: Sangeeta was probably worried and sad for him, having warned him earlier, and this time she made sure he told their mother that evening.

grounding: Shows a student dismissing headaches, irritability and dread before class as weakness, pushing through until motivation collapses in exam week.
